title: Mrs Dalloway
author: Virginia Woolf
written: 1922–24, partly out of an earlier short story
setting: London, Westminster and Regent's Park, on a single Wednesday in June 1923
openingLine: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.
summary: A woman of fifty-two buys flowers, mends a dress and gives a party; a shell-shocked veteran sits in Regent's Park hearing the dead speak and, at six o'clock, throws himself out of a window. The two never meet, and Woolf joins them with clocks, traffic and a phrase from Cymbeline, so that the news of a stranger's death reaches Clarissa in the middle of her own success and she recognises it. The whole book takes one day.
referenceStyle: episode in the day — the novel has no chapters or numbered sections, so quotations are placed by the moment they fall in

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Mrs Dalloway
sourceText.note: The text used runs continuously, without chapter headings or numbered divisions, so references here name the episode. Printed editions mark Woolf's white-space breaks but do not number them.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: By the Hogarth Press, which Woolf ran with her husband and had set type for by hand.

atAGlance.label: Time covered
atAGlance.note: From mid-morning until the small hours, with Big Ben and St Margaret's marking the hours aloud.

atAGlance.label: Earlier title
atAGlance.note: Woolf's working title for the book, and the name of the 1923 short story the novel grew out of.

atAGlance.label: Structure
atAGlance.note: The text runs unbroken except for white space, and the point of view changes inside paragraphs, not between sections.

structure.label: The morning walk
structure.title: Clarissa buys the flowers
structure.summary: Clarissa walks from Westminster to Bond Street for flowers, and the walk keeps opening backwards into Bourton, Peter Walsh and a girl of eighteen at a window. Big Ben strikes; the novel establishes straight away that its present tense is thin and its past is crowded.

structure.label: The motor car and the aeroplane
structure.title: Septimus enters the book
structure.summary: A backfiring car with a blind drawn down, and then an aeroplane writing an advertisement in smoke, are seen at the same moment by people who do not know each other. Woolf uses both to step from one mind to the next, and Septimus Warren Smith enters the book among the onlookers.

structure.label: Regent's Park
structure.title: Rezia and Septimus in the park
structure.summary: Rezia sits with Septimus while he sees Evans coming through the railings and hears sparrows singing in Greek. Her loneliness is given its own sentences: she is an Italian hat-maker in a foreign city with a husband nobody will call ill.

structure.label: Clarissa at home
structure.title: The green dress, and Peter Walsh’s visit
structure.summary: Clarissa learns she has not been asked to Lady Bruton's luncheon, takes her green dress upstairs to mend, and is interrupted by Peter Walsh back from India with a pocket-knife he cannot stop opening. Thirty years of an unfinished argument are conducted in twenty minutes of small talk.

structure.label: Peter walking
structure.title: Peter in the street and the park
structure.summary: Peter leaves the house, invents a romance about a woman in the street, falls asleep in the park and dreams. The section is Woolf's demonstration that the interior life of a failure is as densely furnished as the hostess's, and that both are living mostly in 1890.

structure.label: Septimus, Holmes and Bradshaw
structure.title: Septimus’s war, and Dr Holmes and Sir William Bradshaw
structure.summary: Septimus's history is given: the volunteer, the officer Evans, the death he congratulated himself on not feeling. Dr Holmes prescribes porridge and a music hall; Sir William Bradshaw prescribes six months in a home in the country, and the novel stops to attack him by name.

structure.label: Lady Bruton's luncheon
structure.title: Lady Bruton’s letter to the Times, and Richard’s roses
structure.summary: Richard Dalloway and Hugh Whitbread help Lady Bruton draft a letter to the Times about emigration to Canada. Richard then walks home with roses, intending to say he loves his wife, and does not manage the words.

structure.label: Miss Kilman, Elizabeth and the Strand
structure.title: Elizabeth and Miss Kilman, and the old woman opposite
structure.summary: Doris Kilman, poor, devout and humiliated, takes Elizabeth to the Army and Navy Stores and loses her over an éclair. Elizabeth rides a bus up the Strand thinking about a profession, and Clarissa, alone, watches an old woman in the house opposite go to bed.

structure.label: The window and the ambulance
structure.title: Septimus’s death
structure.summary: Septimus and Rezia trim a hat together in the only untroubled half-hour they are given, and then Dr Holmes comes up the stairs. Peter Walsh, hearing the ambulance from a distance, calls it one of the triumphs of civilisation without knowing what it is carrying.

structure.label: The party
structure.title: Clarissa’s party
structure.summary: The Prime Minister comes; Sally Seton arrives as Lady Rosseter with five sons; Peter waits. The Bradshaws are late because of a case, and Clarissa goes alone into a little room to think about a young man she never met, then returns to her own party.

characters.name: Clarissa Dalloway
characters.role: A politician's wife, fifty-two, giving a party
characters.summary: She is treated by everyone around her, including herself, as a woman who has chosen the shallower life, and the novel spends its day proving that the inner one is not shallow at all. Her defence of parties — that they are an offering, an attempt to bring separate people into relation — is the closest the book comes to a statement of its own purpose.
characters.clue: She goes out for flowers at the start of a June morning and comes back thinking about a girl of eighteen at an open window, thirty-four years ago.

characters.name: Septimus Warren Smith
characters.role: A clerk, decorated in France, thirty years old
characters.summary: He went to war partly to defend a Shakespeare he had read in a Waterloo Road evening class, came back unable to feel anything, and is being treated for that inability by men who regard it as a lack of proportion. What the novel gives him is perception: he is the only character who says out loud what the day is like.
characters.clue: He sits in a park hearing sparrows sing in Greek and watching a dead friend walk through the railings, while his wife tells him to look at the people passing.
characters.firstAppearance: The motor car and the aeroplane

characters.name: Lucrezia Warren Smith
characters.role: Septimus's wife, a hat-maker from Milan
characters.summary: She is twenty-four, in a country where she knows nobody, keeping up appearances for a husband whose illness she is repeatedly told does not exist. Woolf gives her the flattest and most unanswerable sentences in the book, and the one shared half-hour of happiness — trimming a hat together — immediately before the end.
characters.clue: An Italian who came to England for love and now sits on a park bench saying, to nobody, that she is alone.

characters.name: Peter Walsh
characters.role: Back from India, fifty-three, in love with somebody else's wife
characters.summary: He arrives with a pocket-knife he opens and shuts whenever he is nervous, criticises Clarissa's life at length, and then spends the day thinking about nobody else. He is the book's evidence that the road not taken is not obviously the better one.
characters.clue: He sails in from India after five years, cries in a drawing-room within ten minutes, and then follows a stranger through Trafalgar Square making up her life.

characters.name: Richard Dalloway
characters.summary: He carries roses across London meaning to say that he loves his wife, and hands them over without saying it, and the novel treats this as a real event, not a joke. His decency is the quiet argument against Peter's charge that Clarissa married a nonentity.

characters.name: Sally Seton, Lady Rosseter
characters.role: The friend of Clarissa's youth, now married to a mill-owner
characters.summary: At Bourton she smoked cigars, ran naked down a corridor and kissed Clarissa on the terrace — the most exquisite moment of Clarissa's life. She arrives at the party uninvited, with five sons and a large house near Manchester, and the gap between the two versions is one of the things the party is for.

characters.name: Elizabeth Dalloway
characters.summary: Dark, quiet and compared by everyone to a hyacinth or a poplar, she is the one character looking forwards. On a bus up the Strand she considers becoming a doctor or a farmer, which in 1923 is the novel's most concrete piece of hope.

characters.name: Miss Doris Kilman
characters.summary: She lost her teaching post in the war for refusing to say all Germans were villains, has a degree and no money, and has taken refuge in a religion that has not made her kinder. Woolf makes her grasping, self-pitying and entirely explicable, which is harder to read than a straightforward antagonist.

characters.name: Sir William Bradshaw
characters.summary: The son of a shopkeeper who has made himself indispensable, he sees his patients for three-quarters of an hour and prescribes solitude. The novel abandons its usual sympathy to describe the goddesses he serves — Proportion and her sister Conversion — and this is the nearest Woolf comes to naming a villain.
characters.clue: He gives a patient forty-five minutes, calls the cure proportion, and means a home in the country where the man will be kept without friends, books or messages.

characters.name: Lady Bruton
characters.role: A general's daughter with a project about Canada
characters.summary: She invites men to lunch because she needs their prose, not their company, and falls asleep afterwards satisfied that the business has been done. Through her, Woolf shows political influence working through private hospitality — the letter to the Times is composed between the chicken and the coffee.

themes.name: Memory and time
themes.summary: The day is short and the past inside it is enormous: a walk of ten minutes contains a summer at Bourton, a refused proposal and a kiss on a terrace. Woolf's method sets public time, struck aloud by Big Ben, against private time, which expands and contracts according to what is being remembered.
themes.development: Clocks begin as ordinary background, become oppressive around Septimus's appointments, and by the evening the striking hour is the thing that tells Clarissa she has been away from her own party too long.

themes.name: The war
themes.summary: It is five years since the Armistice and everybody has agreed to have recovered. Septimus has not, and the novel makes his symptom — an inability to feel — into an accusation of a society that congratulates itself on the same thing. The dead are mentioned constantly and in passing: a son, a brother, an officer called Evans.
themes.development: Introduced as background to a backfiring car, made explicit in Septimus's history, and finally brought into a Westminster drawing-room as a piece of dinner-party news.

themes.name: Confinement and the asylum
themes.summary: Bradshaw's treatment is rest: no friends, no books, no messages, six months in a home in the country. The novel presents this as force wearing professional clothes, and gives the power a name and a genealogy, so that what looks like medicine is shown to be the enforcement of a norm.
themes.development: Holmes recommends porridge and the music hall; Bradshaw recommends separation; by six o'clock Septimus has decided that the only thing left to him is the window.

themes.name: Isolation
themes.summary: Everybody in the book is alone in a crowd: a wife on a park bench, a returned lover in a hotel room, a poor tutor outside a cathedral, a hostess in a room full of her guests. The party exists because somebody thinks the condition can be temporarily interrupted.
themes.development: Rezia says it out loud in Regent's Park; Clarissa thinks it at her window; and the last movement of the book brings the most isolated figure of all into the middle of the most crowded room, as a story.

themes.name: Performance and sincerity
themes.summary: Clarissa knows exactly how to be a hostess and suspects the skill of being worthless. Richard cannot say what he means; Bradshaw's manner is his method; Kilman's piety is partly a costume for rage. The novel wonders whether a practised surface is a lie, or simply the only way some people have of offering something.
themes.development: The question is posed at the mended dress, sharpened by Peter's contempt for parties, and answered ambiguously in the last pages, where Clarissa's return to the room is presented as both a retreat and an achievement.

themes.name: Class and money
themes.summary: The distance between Clarissa's staircase and Miss Kilman's mackintosh is the book's most reliable measure of feeling. Woolf notices incomes precisely — a tutor's hourly rate, a doctor's fees, Sally's five sons and a house near Manchester — and lets them govern how much of a person the others are willing to see.
themes.development: Comic at Lady Bruton's table, painful in the Army and Navy Stores, and structural at the party, where the Prime Minister's arrival is registered mostly as a change in the noise.

techniques.name: Free indirect style
techniques.definition: Third-person narration that takes on a character's vocabulary and judgements without quotation marks or attribution.
techniques.inThisBook: The exclamations in the first page — what a lark, what a plunge — belong to Clarissa but are printed as narration, so the reader is inside her before being told whose morning this is.

techniques.name: Tunnelling
techniques.definition: Reaching a character’s history by digging back from a present moment, instead of narrating it in order.
techniques.inThisBook: Woolf's own name for the method she worked out while writing this book. Bourton is never given a chapter: it arrives in fragments through whichever mind is currently remembering it, and the fragments do not agree.

techniques.name: Shared events
techniques.definition: A single public incident observed at the same moment by strangers, used to move the narration between minds.
techniques.inThisBook: The car with the drawn blind and the aeroplane writing in smoke each pass through a dozen consciousnesses in a few pages, which lets Woolf change viewpoint without ever leaving the street.

techniques.name: Refrain
techniques.definition: A phrase repeated at intervals, gathering meaning from each new position.
techniques.inThisBook: Two lines of Shakespeare's dirge from Cymbeline surface in Clarissa's mind at a shop window, in Septimus's before the end, and again at the party — the one piece of language the two of them share.

techniques.name: The double plot
techniques.definition: Two parallel stories staged so that each comments on the other.
techniques.inThisBook: Clarissa and Septimus never appear in the same room. Woolf builds the entire novel on the correspondence between them and then delivers it in one sentence at the party, spoken by the doctor who is responsible.

techniques.name: Objects and omens
techniques.definition: Things in the narrative that carry a meaning the characters half-register.
techniques.inThisBook: Peter's pocket-knife, opened and shut whenever he is exposed; Richard's roses, carried across London instead of a sentence; the green dress mended before the party; and the leaden circles the clock leaves in the air.

quotations.text: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.
quotations.context: The first sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: It is reported speech with no speech marks, so the reader arrives in the middle of a household conversation already under way. The name is the formal one, husband's surname and all, and the last word is the only assertion of a self in the sentence — a woman defined by a title choosing to do one small thing alone.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, opening sentence

quotations.text: What a lark! What a plunge!
quotations.context: The June air at the front door recalling a window at Bourton.
quotations.analysis: Two exclamations with no attribution and no verb: the prose has slipped into Clarissa's own idiom within three sentences of the start. 'Plunge' is the word that matters, since it carries both diving into the morning and going under, and the novel will use water for both all day.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, opening pages

quotations.text: In people’s eyes, in the swing, tramp, and trudge; in the bellow and the uproar; the carriages, motorcars, omnibuses, vans, sandwich men shuffling and swinging; brass bands; barrel organs; in the triumph and the jingle and the strange high singing of some aeroplane overhead was what she loved; life; London; this moment of June.
quotations.context: Crossing Victoria Street on the way to the flower shop.
quotations.analysis: The sentence withholds its verb for forty words, so the noise accumulates before anything is said about it, and then the last three items are stripped to bare nouns separated by semicolons. 'This moment of June' is the smallest of the three and the one that will be gone by the evening.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, opening pages

quotations.text: The leaden circles dissolved in the air.
quotations.context: Big Ben striking, early in the day.
quotations.analysis: The clock is described as a shape with weight, spreading and vanishing, so the passing of an hour is something the reader can watch disappear. The sentence returns unchanged several times, and by the last occurrence it arrives just after a death, which is how a refrain acquires a meaning it did not start with.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, opening pages

quotations.text: She had a perpetual sense, as she watched the taxi cabs, of being out, out, far out to sea and alone; she always had the feeling that it was very, very dangerous to live even one day.
quotations.context: Clarissa on her own habit of standing apart from what she is in the middle of.
quotations.analysis: The image arrives while she is looking at traffic, which is the point: nothing has happened. Both halves double a word — out, out; very, very — so the sentence sounds like someone insisting on something they cannot get anyone to take seriously, and the novel will spend the day proving that one day can indeed be fatal.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, opening pages

quotations.text: Fear no more the heat o’ the sun Nor the furious winter’s rages.
quotations.context: Read off an open book in a Hatchards window.
quotations.analysis: The lines are from the funeral song in Cymbeline, and Clarissa picks them up as consolation without dwelling on the fact that they are sung over a body. Septimus will arrive at the same words independently, which is the first evidence that the two plots are running on one text.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, opening pages

quotations.text: She had the oddest sense of being herself invisible; unseen; unknown
quotations.context: On being, at fifty-two, Mrs Richard Dalloway and nothing else.
quotations.analysis: Three words for the same condition, each a shade further from company, separated by semicolons so that they read as a slow settling, not a list. The feeling is presented as odd, not distressing, which is more disturbing than a complaint would be.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, opening pages

quotations.text: The world has raised its whip; where will it descend?
quotations.reference: The motor car and the aeroplane
quotations.context: Septimus's first appearance, held up in the crowd around the stopped car.
quotations.analysis: It is printed as a separate paragraph, unattributed and in the present tense, so it reads as a general statement before the reader realises it is a symptom. The crowd around him is speculating about royalty; he is the only person there who has been where the whip already fell.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, the scene of the motor car

quotations.text: I am alone; I am alone!
quotations.speaker: Lucrezia Warren Smith
quotations.context: By the fountain, having left Septimus on the seat.
quotations.analysis: The repetition is the sound of somebody with nobody to say it to, and the sentence has no listener inside the novel at all. Woolf places it in the middle of the most public space in the book, a park full of people, and the paragraph around it widens to Roman roads and ancient marshland — loneliness given geological scale.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, the Regent's Park scene

quotations.text: He woke with extreme suddenness, saying to himself, “The death of the soul.”
quotations.context: Peter waking from a doze on a seat in Regent's Park.
quotations.analysis: The phrase arrives before its object does; only afterwards does he attach it to a scene at Bourton where Clarissa was rude about a neighbour's affair. Woolf shows a judgement forming as a sensation first and an argument second, which is how most of the novel's opinions about people are made.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Peter Walsh in Regent's Park

quotations.text: The compensation of growing old, Peter Walsh thought, coming out of Regent’s Park, and holding his hat in hand, was simply this; that the passions remain as strong as ever
quotations.context: Leaving the park in the early afternoon.
quotations.analysis: He is fifty-three, in love with a married woman he refuses to admit he is in love with, and calls the persistence of feeling a compensation. The novel lets the claim stand and then follows him through an entire day of proving its second half — that age brings the power to handle what one feels — false.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Peter Walsh leaving Regent's Park

quotations.text: He had gone through the whole show, friendship, European War, death, had won promotion, was still under thirty and was bound to survive.
quotations.context: Septimus's history: the volunteer who congratulated himself on feeling nothing.
quotations.analysis: Four years are itemised as a list with commas, in which a friendship, a continental war and a death carry equal weight and none carries any. 'The whole show' is the language soldiers used, and here it is doing exactly the work it was invented for — making an experience small enough to carry.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Septimus's history

quotations.text: He had not cared when Evans was killed; that was worst
quotations.context: The charge Septimus brings against himself in the small hours.
quotations.analysis: The crime he cannot forgive is an absence, not an act, and the two-word verdict at the end is delivered in his own voice without any narrator softening it. The whole medical apparatus of the novel is engaged in treating a man for a failure of feeling that he has already identified more accurately than either doctor.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Septimus's history

quotations.text: Once you fall, Septimus repeated to himself, human nature is on you. Holmes and Bradshaw are on you.
quotations.context: After Sir William has decided on a home in the country.
quotations.analysis: The two doctors are named in the same breath as human nature and given the same grammar — something that is 'on you', like weather or a pack. Woolf has made the medical profession into a hunting metaphor, and the sentence explains why, an hour later, a man will prefer a window to a waiting room.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, after the Harley Street consultation

quotations.text: Proportion, divine proportion, Sir William’s goddess
quotations.context: The narrator stepping aside to describe what Bradshaw actually worships.
quotations.analysis: The novel abandons any single consciousness here and speaks in its own voice, capitalising an abstraction into a deity with a biography — hospitals walked, salmon caught, a son begotten in Harley Street. Making a medical principle into a goddess lets Woolf treat a professional opinion as a religion with converts and casualties.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, the passage on Sir William Bradshaw

quotations.text: Conversion is her name and she feasts on the wills of the weakly, loving to impress, to impose, adoring her own features stamped on the face of the populace.
quotations.context: Proportion's less presentable sister, named a page later.
quotations.analysis: The verbs escalate from impress to impose, and the last image — a face stamped on a population like a head on a coin — puts missionary work, empire and psychiatric care in a single frame. This is the most openly political sentence in the novel, and it is aimed at a doctor with excellent manners.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, the passage on Sir William Bradshaw

quotations.text: order rest in bed; rest in solitude; silence and rest; rest without friends, without books, without messages
quotations.context: Sir William's prescription, described by the narrator in his own idiom.
quotations.analysis: The word 'rest' appears four times in a single clause and each repetition takes something else away, so that a comfort is converted into a deprivation by accumulation alone. Read the list as a description of a room, not a treatment, and it is a cell, which is the reading the sentence is built to produce.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, the passage on Sir William Bradshaw

quotations.text: (But he could not bring himself to say he loved her; not in so many words.)
quotations.context: Richard arriving home with roses he has carried across London for that purpose.
quotations.analysis: Woolf puts the most important fact of the marriage inside brackets, which is exactly the status it has in the marriage. The reader knows what the flowers were rehearsed to say and Clarissa does not, and the novel treats that ordinary failure with the same seriousness it gives to a death.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Richard Dalloway bringing the roses

quotations.text: love and religion would destroy that, whatever it was, the privacy of the soul
quotations.reference: Miss Kilman, Elizabeth and the Strand
quotations.context: Clarissa at the window, watching the old woman in the house opposite.
quotations.analysis: The two forces usually credited with saving people are here named as the two most likely to invade them, and the grammar hesitates — 'whatever it was' — because she cannot define the thing she is defending. It is the nearest Clarissa comes to a creed, and she arrives at it while looking through a window at a stranger going to bed.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Clarissa at the window

quotations.text: here was one room; there another. Did religion solve that, or love?
quotations.reference: Miss Kilman, Elizabeth and the Strand
quotations.context: The same passage, stating the problem the old woman opposite represents.
quotations.analysis: The supreme mystery is reduced to a matter of architecture: two rooms, and no way through the wall. Posing it as a question with two candidate answers and no verdict is characteristic — the novel prefers to leave the problem standing and let a party be the provisional reply.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Clarissa at the window

quotations.text: Holmes was coming upstairs. Holmes would burst open the door.
quotations.context: The last minute of Septimus's life, alone in the sitting room.
quotations.analysis: Two short sentences beginning with the same name, one in the past continuous and one in the conditional: the doctor is already here and about to arrive. Septimus then considers a bread knife, the gas and a razor before the window, so the death is the last item on a list of shut doors, not an impulse.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, the death of Septimus

quotations.text: Death was defiance. Death was an attempt to communicate; people feeling the impossibility of reaching the centre which, mystically, evaded them; closeness drew apart
quotations.context: Clarissa alone in a small room, having been told of the young man's suicide.
quotations.analysis: She reaches an interpretation of a stranger's death by way of her own life, and the sentence turns from statement to explanation without a break. The clause about closeness drawing apart covers her marriage, her lost friendship with Sally and her own party, and she does not notice that she has changed the subject.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Clarissa's withdrawal during the party

quotations.text: She felt glad that he had done it; thrown it away while they went on living.
quotations.context: The same scene, a moment before she returns to her guests.
quotations.analysis: 'Glad' is the word the novel risks everything on, and the semicolon does the work: the act is named only as 'it', twice, and never as death. Setting his throwing away against their going on living makes survival, not suicide, the thing that requires justifying.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Clarissa's withdrawal during the party

quotations.text: It is Clarissa, he said. For there she was.
quotations.context: The last two sentences of the novel, in Peter Walsh's mind.
quotations.analysis: After a day of remembering her, the answer turns out to be her presence, and the novel ends on the verb ‘was’: past tense at the exact moment of arrival. There is no dialogue, no meeting and no resolution: a man identifies the source of his own terror and ecstasy, and the book stops.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, closing sentences

timeline.label: Virginia Stephen born in Kensington
timeline.detail: Into a large literary household; her father Leslie Stephen edited the Dictionary of National Biography.

timeline.label: Her mother dies
timeline.detail: The first of the bereavements that were followed by breakdowns, and the beginning of her own long history with doctors.

timeline.label: The Voyage Out published
timeline.detail: Her first novel, in which a Mr and Mrs Dalloway appear as passengers.

timeline.label: The Hogarth Press founded
timeline.detail: Set up by Leonard and Virginia Woolf with a hand press, which eventually meant she published herself and answered to no editor.

timeline.label: The Armistice
timeline.detail: Less than five years before the June day in 1923 that the novel describes, and still the event everybody in it is organised around.

timeline.label: Jacob's Room published
timeline.detail: The first of her novels to abandon conventional plotting, and the book that made this one possible.

timeline.label: The War Office committee on shell-shock reports
timeline.detail: Its evidence and recommendations were argued over publicly while Woolf was writing Septimus.

timeline.label: 'Mrs Dalloway in Bond Street' appears
timeline.detail: The short story out of which the novel grew, and which supplied its opening walk.

timeline.label: Mrs Dalloway published on 14 May
timeline.detail: By the Hogarth Press, with a jacket designed by Vanessa Bell.

timeline.label: Woolf's The Common Reader published
timeline.detail: Her first collection of essays, which set out in criticism the case her fiction was making in practice.

timeline.label: Woolf's To the Lighthouse published
timeline.detail: The next novel, which takes the method of this one and stretches it across ten years and one empty house.

timeline.label: Woolf drowns herself in the River Ouse
timeline.detail: At fifty-nine, in Sussex, during the second war.

places.name: Westminster
places.note: Where Clarissa lives and where Big Ben strikes the hours the whole novel is measured by.

places.name: Bond Street
places.note: The flower shop at the end of the morning walk, and the street where the motor car stops.

places.name: Regent's Park
places.note: Where Rezia sits with Septimus, and where Peter Walsh falls asleep on a seat.

places.name: Harley Street
places.note: Sir William Bradshaw's consulting room, and the clock that shreds the hour into slices.

places.name: The Strand
places.note: Where Elizabeth's omnibus takes her, past the Temple, thinking about a profession.

places.name: Victoria Street
places.note: Crossed early in the walk, and the setting of the novel's first great catalogue of London noise.

criticalViews.summary: The oldest reading takes the book as a technical achievement first: a way of writing thought that moves between minds without announcement, and of making a single day hold a lifetime.
criticalViews.counter: Treated purely as method, the novel loses its anger: the pages on Bradshaw are an attack.

criticalViews.position: A war novel in civilian clothes
criticalViews.summary: Septimus is the book’s evidence, not a subplot: the Armistice is five years old, everyone has agreed to be recovered, and the novel puts a casualty of that agreement in the middle of a fashionable London day.
criticalViews.counter: It can flatten Clarissa into a foil, when her own resistance to being explained is what the last pages are about.

criticalViews.summary: Readings drawing on Woolf's own experience of rest cures treat Holmes and Bradshaw as the novel's real antagonists, and the language of proportion and conversion as an account of how power dresses itself as care.
criticalViews.counter: Woolf gives Bradshaw no interior life at all, which is the one place the novel declines to extend its own method.

criticalViews.position: A book about love between women
criticalViews.summary: Criticism since the 1970s has taken the kiss on the terrace at Bourton as the emotional centre, and read Clarissa’s marriage and her party as what she built afterwards.
criticalViews.counter: The novel is careful never to settle it, and Sally's arrival with a husband and five sons is part of that care.

essayQuestions.question: How does Woolf connect Clarissa Dalloway and Septimus Warren Smith?
plan: Establish that they never meet, and list the mechanisms that join them: clocks, the motor car, the aeroplane, and two lines of Cymbeline.
Track the shared language — fear no more, the sense of a plunge, the privacy of the soul — and show it arriving independently in each.
Examine how the news actually reaches Clarissa: as dinner-party conversation, brought by the doctor responsible.
Read her response closely, especially the word 'glad' and the refusal to name the act.
Decide what the novel gains by keeping them apart, and what it would lose from a meeting.

essayQuestions.question: 'The most political thing in Mrs Dalloway is a doctor's good manners.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Medicine, authority and the treatment of Septimus
plan: Set Holmes and Bradshaw side by side: porridge and the music hall against six months of solitude.
Analyse the passage on Proportion and Conversion, noting where the narration leaves every character's mind.
Show how the prescription is built by repetition, and what each repetition removes.
Connect the language of conversion to empire and religion, which the passage explicitly invokes.
Consider whether the attack is weakened by the fact that Bradshaw is never given an interior life.

essayQuestions.question: What does Woolf's handling of time achieve in Mrs Dalloway?
essayQuestions.focus: Clocks, memory and a single day
plan: Separate the two clocks: Big Ben's public hours, and the private time that expands inside a moment.
Use the opening walk to show a ten-minute journey containing thirty-four years.
Examine the leaden circles as a refrain, and what changes each time it returns.
Contrast Harley Street, where time is sliced and sold, with Bourton, which has no chronology at all.
Assess what confining the book to one day forces Woolf to do that a conventional chronology would not.

essayQuestions.question: Is Clarissa's party a triumph or an evasion?
plan: Gather the charges: Peter's contempt, Kilman's resentment, and Clarissa's own suspicion that she does it out of vanity.
Set against them her account of a party as an offering, and of the problem of one room and then another.
Weigh the moment she leaves the party for the little room, and what she does with the news there.
Read the return to the guests as either a retreat or a decision, using the final lines as evidence.
Reach a judgement about whether the novel endorses her answer or merely declines to supply a better one.

discussionQuestions: Clarissa and Septimus never meet. Why does the novel insist on that?
Is 'glad' the right word for what Clarissa feels about a stranger's suicide, and what would be lost if Woolf had chosen a safer one?
Bradshaw is courteous, successful and never cruel in anything he says. Why is he the nearest thing the book has to a villain?
Richard cannot say he loves his wife and brings roses instead. Does the novel treat that as a failure?
The book covers one day and ends without a meeting or a resolution. What has changed by the last page?
